prerequisites: Competencies taught in the Machine Learning modules and either Foundations of Statistics or Elementary Stochastics are recommended.

learning_outcomes.text: Students can describe the technical perspective on Natural Language Processing (NLP), i.e., the field of Artificial Intelligence that deals with the processing and understanding of human language.
Students can explain methods for developing computer software that understands and processes human language.
Students can explain modern data-driven approaches, with a focus on machine learning techniques.
Students can apply their knowledge in group work on real NLP projects.

Students are able to develop their own systems that interpret written language. The covered applications vary in complexity and include, for example, Entity Recognition, Sentiment Analysis, Semantic Similarity, and Question Answering.

syllabus_topics: Overview of the goals, challenges, and applications of NLP
Converting words to their base forms (tokenization, stemming, lemmatization)
Algorithms for text classification and methods for measuring and evaluating the performance of these algorithms
Use of lexical resources in NLP
Syntactic analysis (Part of Speech Tagging, Chunking and Parsing)
Techniques for extracting meaning from text (semantic analysis)

NLP applications (e.g., document similarity, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, question answering, summarization, fake news detection, plagiarism detection, abusive language detection, opinion mining)
teaching_methods: Internship with high computer science content

assessment_methods.method: Oral presentation of solutions to at least two exercise assignments

assessment_rules: To acquire credit points, students must achieve at least 50 percent of the points from the weekly exercise assignments and orally present the solution to at least two of them. The final grade is based on two partial examinations: a written exam (3 LP) and a written elaboration (3 LP). Grading is done on a scale of 0 to 15 points according to the examination regulations for the M.Sc. Data Science degree program.
bibliography: Eisenstein, Jacob. "Introduction to natural language processing. MIT press", (2019).
Jurafsky, Daniel, and James H. Martin. "Speech and Language Processing: An Introduction to Natural Language Processing, Computational Linguistics, and Speech Recognition." (2000).
